query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The native oxide film on pre-exposure Q235 steel forms a protective, self-healing barrier at room temperature but undergoes destabilization, fluxing, and spallation under high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt exposures, thereby switching from corrosion protection to accelerated degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state with its native microstructure and naturally formed iron oxide (primarily Fe3O4) film.
generation.intervention: Expose identical sets of Q235 steel samples to two environments: one set under room-temperature saline conditions and another set under aggressive salt exposure at high temperatures (700–900 °C). Optionally, include a controlled annealing step to standardize the native oxide film on some samples.
generation.conditions: The hypothesis applies under conditions where an aggressive salt (e.g., a molten salt or high chloride solution) interacts with the oxide layer at elevated temperatures, causing thermal stresses and enhanced diffusion. It should not apply in inert high-temperature environments or in room-temperature conditions where the native oxide remains adherent and self-healing.
generation.structural_mediator: The native iron oxide film (Fe3O4) on Q235 steel and its adhesion/stability at the metal–oxide interface.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the native oxide film forms a continuous and self-repairing barrier against further corrosion; however, when exposed to high-temperature aggressive salts, thermal expansion mismatch and salt-induced chemical fluxing lead to destabilization and spallation of the oxide layer, exposing the underlying metal to accelerated corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature salt exposure, Q235 steel will exhibit a significantly higher mass loss and observable degradation (e.g., spalled or discontinuous oxide layer, pitting, and increased corrosion rates) compared to its behavior under room-temperature salt exposure or compared to a reference material (e.g., a Cr-rich stainless steel with a stable passivation film).
generation.baseline: Q235 steel maintained under inert or mildly corrosive conditions (such as room-temperature exposures or high-temperature environments without aggressive salts) where the native oxide film remains intact.
generation.boundary: This mechanism may not apply if the steel is pre-modified (e.g., alloyed with protective elements such as Cr or Nb) to form a more robust passivation film, or if the salt environment lacks the chemical activity necessary to induce oxide fluxing at high temperature.
generation.uncertainty: The detailed kinetics and composition changes of the native oxide film on Q235 steel under varying thermal and salt exposure conditions remain not fully characterized. The relative contributions of thermal stress versus salt chemistry in oxide destabilization need further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare Q235 steel samples with uniform surface finish to ensure comparable native oxide formation. Divide samples into three groups: (i) exposed to room-temperature salt environment, (ii) exposed to high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt environment, and (iii) a control group with a pre-engineered protective Cr-rich oxide layer. Monitor and compare mass loss, oxide morphology, and corrosion rates over identical exposure times.
measurements: Oxide film morphology and spallation (via SEM and XPS)
Phase composition of the oxide (using XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Q235 steel samples exposed to high-temperature salt do not exhibit significantly higher mass loss, oxide film spallation, and higher corrosion rates compared to both room-temperature exposed samples and the control with a protective Cr-rich oxide, then the hypothesis that thermal and salt-induced destabilization of the native oxide drives accelerated degradation is falsified.

## Abstract
In this paper, the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating with a thickness of 500 μm on Q235 steel substrate was fabricated by plasma spraying. The microscopic results showed that a new Laves phase is formed in the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating compared to the HEA powder, and elemental segregation occurs between the dendrites and the interdendrites of the coating, while the interdendritic phase enriches with the Cr and Nb. The phase composition change and elemental segregation behavior were mainly due to the faster cooling rate of the plasma spraying technique. At the junction of the coating and the substrate, the HEA coating bonded well to the substrate; in addition, the width of transition zone was merely 2 μm. The microhardness of the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating was 321 HV0.5, which is significantly higher than that of the substrate. In terms of corrosion resistance, the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating has good corrosion resistance in NaCl solution. Although the corrosion form was pitting corrosion, the pitting potential of the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating was significantly higher than that of other coatings, which was mainly because of the dense passivation film

## Abstract
AbstractThe corrosion behavior of the FCC Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 high entropy alloy (HEA) after exposure to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours, has been investigated. Results show that the HEA lost a higher mass compared to the reference 316 H stainless steel due to the dissolution of Mn into the molten salt. The loss of Mn from the alloy appeared to discourage the dissolution of Cr in the molten fluoride salts which is widely recognized as the mechanism of corrosion degradation. Thermal exposure at 700 °C for 1000 hours also led to the precipitation of an additional BCC phase Cr67Fe13Mn18.5Ni1.5, which was confirmed by CALPHAD predictions.Subject terms: Structural materials, Metals and alloys
## Introduction
Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr2O3), alumina (Al2O3) or silica (SiO2) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation.
